meta.subject: Chemistry
meta.notes: Level 3 is NCERT-hard (constructed beyond textbook difficulty but within syllabus), not JEE-hard. Bonus questions mix concepts across topics; unlock after Level 3 or as challenge round.
meta.rendering: Text fields contain lightweight HTML (<sup>, <sub>, entities, and <span class="nuc"> for stacked isotope notation). Render with innerHTML/dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Required CSS: .nuc{display:inline-block;text-align:right;line-height:1;vertical-align:-0.35em;} .nuc span{display:block;font-size:0.62em;}
meta.topic_drill: Topic drill mode: filter questions by topic across all levels, order L1->L2->L3, serve in sets of ~6. Each topic has a concept card in the 'topics' array (summary, key_formulas, worked_example, common_mistakes) shown via a 'See concept' button. Topic names in 'topics' match question 'topic' tags exactly for lookup. After a failed level, link weak topics to their drill + concept card.

questions.question: In a cathode ray discharge tube, the rays travel from:
questions.explanation: Cathode rays are streams of electrons; they start at the negative electrode (cathode) and move toward the positive anode.
questions.hint: The rays are named after where they start.

questions.question: Cathode rays consist of:
questions.explanation: Their deflection in electric/magnetic fields matches negatively charged particles — electrons.
questions.hint: They bend toward the positive plate.

questions.question: The charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) of the electron was determined by:
questions.explanation: J.J. Thomson (1897) measured e/m = 1.758820 × 10<sup>11</sup> C/kg by balancing electric and magnetic deflections in a cathode ray tube.
questions.hint: Cathode ray tube with crossed fields.

questions.question: The charge on the electron was determined by Millikan using the:
questions.explanation: Millikan's oil drop experiment (1906-14) showed the charge on any droplet is always n x e, giving e = -1.602 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C.
questions.hint: Tiny charged droplets balanced against gravity.

questions.question: The accepted charge on an electron is:
questions.explanation: e = -1.602176 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C. The other numbers are the electron's mass, the neutron's mass, and Planck's constant — different quantities entirely.
questions.hint: It's a charge, measured in coulombs.

questions.question: The mass of an electron is approximately:
questions.explanation: m<sub>e</sub> = 9.1094 × 10<sup>−31</sup> kg, about 1/1836 of a proton's mass.
questions.hint: It is far lighter than a proton.

questions.question: Neutrons were discovered by Chadwick by bombarding a thin sheet of beryllium with:
questions.explanation: Chadwick (1932) bombarded beryllium with α particles; electrically neutral particles slightly heavier than protons were emitted — neutrons.
questions.hint: The same particles Rutherford used for scattering.

questions.question: The proton was obtained as the smallest and lightest positive ion from:
questions.explanation: Ionizing hydrogen gives H<sup>+</sup>, the lightest positive ion — the proton, characterised in 1919.
questions.hint: The simplest atom.

questions.question: Which fundamental particle has no charge?
questions.explanation: The neutron has zero charge; electron is -1, proton +1, and an α particle carries +2.
questions.hint: Its name gives it away.

questions.question: The approximate mass of a proton in atomic mass units (u) is:
questions.explanation: Proton mass is about 1.00727 u; 1/1836 u is roughly the electron's mass relative to a proton.
questions.hint: Protons and neutrons each count as about one unit.

questions.question: Thomson's model of the atom is popularly called the:
questions.explanation: Thomson pictured a uniform sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded like plums in a pudding (or seeds in a watermelon).
questions.hint: Think of fruit in a dessert.

questions.question: In Thomson's model, the mass of the atom is assumed to be:
questions.explanation: Thomson assumed mass and positive charge spread evenly over the whole atomic sphere — exactly what Rutherford's experiment later disproved.
questions.hint: Opposite of the nuclear picture.

questions.question: Rutherford's famous scattering experiment used a thin foil of:
questions.explanation: A ~100 nm thick gold foil was bombarded with α particles; gold can be beaten extremely thin.
questions.hint: The most malleable metal.

questions.question: In Rutherford's experiment, roughly what fraction of α particles bounced back by nearly 180°?
questions.explanation: Only ~1 in 20,000 bounced back — showing that the positive charge occupies a very tiny volume (the nucleus).
questions.hint: It was an extremely rare event.

questions.question: The radius of an atom is about 10<sup>−10</sup> m. The radius of its nucleus is about:
questions.explanation: Nucleus ~10<sup>−15</sup> m vs atom ~10<sup>−10</sup> m — 100,000 times smaller. If the nucleus were a cricket ball, the atom would be ~5 km wide.
questions.hint: Five orders of magnitude smaller than the atom.

questions.question: According to Rutherford's model, electrons and the nucleus are held together by:
questions.explanation: The negative electrons are attracted to the positive nucleus by coulombic (electrostatic) attraction.
questions.hint: Opposite charges attract.

questions.question: Rutherford's model could NOT explain:
options: The positive charge of the nucleus
questions.explanation: Per Maxwell's theory, an accelerating electron should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus in ~10<sup>−8</sup> s — so the model can't explain why atoms are stable.
questions.hint: An orbiting charge should radiate energy.

questions.question: The atomic number (Z) of an element equals the number of:
questions.explanation: Z = number of protons in the nucleus (= number of electrons in a neutral atom).
questions.hint: The count that defines the element.

questions.question: The mass number (A) of an atom equals:
questions.explanation: A = protons (Z) + neutrons (n). Protons and neutrons together are called nucleons.
questions.hint: Count everything in the nucleus.

questions.question: Protons and neutrons present in the nucleus are collectively called:
questions.explanation: Particles residing in the nucleus — protons and neutrons — are nucleons; their total is the mass number.
questions.hint: Named after where they live.

questions.question: Atoms with the same atomic number but different mass numbers are called:
questions.explanation: Isotopes: same Z (same element), different A due to different neutron counts — e.g. <sup>12</sup>C, <sup>13</sup>C, <sup>14</sup>C.
questions.hint: Same element, different mass.

questions.question: <sup>14</sup>C (Z=6) and <sup>14</sup>N (Z=7) are examples of:
questions.explanation: Same mass number (14) but different atomic numbers — that is the definition of isobars.
questions.hint: Compare their mass numbers.

questions.question: The isotope of hydrogen containing 1 proton and 2 neutrons is:
questions.explanation: Tritium (<sup>3</sup>T): 1 proton + 2 neutrons, A = 3. Deuterium has 1 neutron; protium has none.
questions.hint: Its mass number is 3.

questions.question: All isotopes of a given element show the same chemical behaviour because they have the same number of:
questions.explanation: Chemical properties are controlled by electrons (determined by protons); neutron count has almost no effect on chemistry.
questions.hint: Chemistry happens in the electron cloud.

questions.question: The speed of all electromagnetic radiations in vacuum is:
questions.explanation: In vacuum every EM wave — radio to gamma — travels at c = 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s regardless of wavelength.
questions.hint: Same speed for all of them.
distractor_logic: true in a medium, not vacuum

questions.question: Frequency (ν), wavelength (λ) and the speed of light (c) are related by:
questions.explanation: c = ν x λ: waves per second times length per wave gives distance per second.
questions.hint: Multiply how many waves pass per second by each wave's length.

questions.question: The SI unit of frequency is:
questions.explanation: Frequency is waves passing a point per second — hertz (Hz = s<sup>−1</sup>), named after Heinrich Hertz.
questions.hint: Named after a physicist.

questions.question: Wavenumber is defined as:
options: Number of wavelengths per unit length
Number of waves passing a point per second
questions.explanation: Wavenumber = 1/λ, the number of wavelengths per unit length; common unit cm<sup>−1</sup>.
questions.hint: It is the reciprocal of wavelength.

questions.question: Unlike sound waves, electromagnetic waves:
options: Do not require a medium and can travel in vacuum
questions.explanation: EM waves are oscillating electric and magnetic fields; they need no medium — light from the Sun crosses vacuum to reach us.
questions.hint: Sunlight reaches Earth through empty space.

questions.question: The smallest quantity of energy that can be emitted or absorbed as electromagnetic radiation is called a:
questions.explanation: Planck named the smallest discrete packet of EM energy a 'quantum'; for light, the quantum is called a photon.
questions.hint: Planck coined the term in 1900.

questions.question: According to Planck, the energy of a quantum of radiation is:
questions.explanation: E = h ν: energy is directly proportional to frequency, with Planck's constant h as the proportionality constant.
questions.hint: Higher frequency, higher energy.

questions.question: The value of Planck's constant h is:
questions.explanation: h = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s. The others are the electron charge, electron mass, and speed of light — wrong quantities and wrong units.
questions.hint: The smallest of these numbers.

questions.question: The photoelectric effect is the ejection of ______ when light of suitable frequency strikes a metal surface.
questions.explanation: Hertz (1887) observed electrons ejected from metals like K, Rb, Cs when exposed to light — the photoelectric effect.
questions.hint: The lightest particle leaves first.

questions.question: The minimum frequency below which no photoelectric effect occurs is called the:
questions.explanation: Threshold frequency &ν;<sub>0</sub>: below it, no electrons are ejected no matter how intense the light.
questions.hint: The 'doorstep' the light must cross.

questions.question: Line emission spectra can identify unknown elements just like ______ identify people.
questions.explanation: Each element has a unique line spectrum — the NCERT compares them to fingerprints. Bunsen first used line spectra to identify elements.
questions.hint: Unique to each individual.
distractor_logic: the textbook's exact analogy is different

questions.question: Which element was discovered in the Sun by spectroscopic methods?
questions.explanation: Helium ('helios' = Sun) was detected in the solar spectrum before being found on Earth. Rb, Cs, Tl, In, Ga, Sc were found via spectroscopy of minerals.
questions.hint: Its name comes from the Greek word for Sun.
distractor_logic: found in minerals, not the Sun

questions.question: The Balmer series of the hydrogen spectrum lies in the ______ region.
questions.explanation: Balmer lines (n<sub>2</sub> → n<sub>1</sub>=2) are the only hydrogen lines in the visible region; Lyman is UV, Paschen/Brackett/Pfund are IR.
questions.hint: It's the series our eyes can see.

questions.question: According to Bohr, the angular momentum of an electron in a stationary state is:
questions.explanation: Bohr's quantisation condition: m<sub>e</sub> v r = n(h/2π), n = 1, 2, 3... Only orbits satisfying this are allowed.
questions.hint: It is quantised in units of h/2π.

questions.question: The de Broglie relation connecting wavelength and momentum is:
questions.explanation: λ = h/mv = h/p: every moving particle has an associated wavelength inversely proportional to its momentum.
questions.hint: Heavier and faster means shorter wavelength.

questions.question: The shape of an s orbital is:
questions.explanation: All s orbitals are spherically symmetric — the probability of finding the electron at a given distance is equal in all directions.
questions.hint: Same in every direction.

questions.question: The number of protons and neutrons in 8035Br are respectively:
questions.explanation: Z = 35 protons; neutrons = A - Z = 80 - 35 = 45.
questions.hint: Subtract the atomic number from the mass number.

questions.question: A species has 18 electrons, 16 protons and 16 neutrons. It is:
questions.explanation: 16 protons = sulphur. Electrons (18) exceed protons by 2, so it is the anion S<sup>2−</sup> with mass number 32.
questions.hint: Compare electron and proton counts first.

questions.question: Which pair is isoelectronic (same number of electrons)?
questions.explanation: Na<sup>+</sup> = 11-1 = 10 e; Mg<sup>2+</sup> = 12-2 = 10 e. K<sup>+</sup> has 18 e and S<sup>2−</sup> has 18 e, so those pair with each other, not with Na<sup>+</sup>.
questions.hint: Subtract the charge from Z for each ion.

questions.question: Yellow light from a sodium lamp has wavelength 580 nm. Its frequency is about:
questions.explanation: ν = c/λ = (3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup>)/(580 × 10<sup>−9</sup>) = 5.17 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz.
questions.hint: Divide c by the wavelength in metres.

questions.question: The wavenumber of yellow radiation of wavelength 5800 Å is about:
questions.explanation: wavenumber = 1/λ = 1/(5800 × 10<sup>−10</sup> m) = 1.724 × 10<sup>6</sup> m<sup>−1</sup> (= 1.724 × 10<sup>4</sup> cm<sup>−1</sup>).
questions.hint: Take the reciprocal of the wavelength in metres.

questions.question: The energy of one photon of radiation with frequency 5 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz is:
questions.explanation: E = h ν = (6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup>)(5 × 10<sup>14</sup>) = 3.313 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J.
questions.hint: Multiply Planck's constant by the frequency.

questions.question: The energy of one MOLE of photons of frequency 5 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz is about:
questions.explanation: Per photon E = 3.313 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J; per mole = 3.313 × 10<sup>−19</sup> × 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> = 1.995 × 10<sup>5</sup> J = 199.5 kJ.
questions.hint: Multiply the single-photon energy by Avogadro's number.

questions.question: The visible spectrum in frequency terms extends approximately from:
questions.explanation: Violet 400 nm gives 7.5 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz and red 750 nm gives 4.0 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz.
questions.hint: Convert 400-750 nm using ν = c/λ.
distractor_logic: wavelengths in nm quoted as Hz

questions.question: Intense red light shone on potassium for hours ejects no electrons, but weak yellow light works instantly, because:
options: Red light's frequency is below the threshold frequency of potassium
questions.explanation: For K, &ν;<sub>0</sub> = 5.0 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz. Red light (4.3-4.6 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz) is below threshold; no single photon has enough energy, and intensity cannot compensate.
questions.hint: It's about energy per photon, not total energy.

questions.question: In the photoelectric effect, the NUMBER of electrons ejected is proportional to the:
questions.explanation: More photons (higher intensity) eject more electrons; frequency instead controls the kinetic energy of each ejected electron.
questions.hint: More photons means more ejections.

questions.question: The kinetic energy of an ejected photoelectron equals:
questions.explanation: KE = h ν - h &ν;<sub>0</sub>: photon energy minus the work function (minimum energy to eject the electron).
questions.hint: Photon energy minus the escape cost.

questions.question: The threshold frequency of potassium is 5.0 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz. Its work function is about:
questions.explanation: W<sub>0</sub> = h &ν;<sub>0</sub> = (6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup>)(5.0 × 10<sup>14</sup>) = 3.31 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J (about 2.07 eV).
questions.hint: Work function is h times threshold frequency.

questions.question: In the HYDROGEN atom, the energy of an orbital depends only on:
questions.explanation: For H (and one-electron ions), energy depends only on the principal quantum number n; 2s and 2p are degenerate. In multi-electron atoms it depends on n and l.
questions.hint: One-electron systems are special.

questions.question: Orbitals having the same energy are called:
questions.explanation: Degenerate = equal energy, e.g. the three 2p orbitals, or 2s and 2p in the hydrogen atom.
questions.hint: A specific technical term from the chapter.

questions.question: In the Balmer series formula, the lines correspond to transitions ending at n<sub>1</sub> =
questions.explanation: Balmer: electron falls to n = 2 from n = 3, 4, 5... These are hydrogen's visible lines. n<sub>1</sub> = 1 is Lyman, n<sub>1</sub> = 3 is Paschen.
questions.hint: The visible series.

questions.question: The value 109,677 cm<sup>−1</sup> is known as the:
questions.explanation: The Rydberg constant appears in wavenumber = 109677(1/n<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> - 1/n<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>) cm<sup>−1</sup>, describing all hydrogen line series.
questions.hint: It appears in the hydrogen spectrum formula.

questions.question: When an excited electron of a hydrogen atom in n = 6 drops to the ground state, the maximum number of emission lines is:
questions.explanation: Number of lines = n(n-1)/2 = 6 × 5/2 = 15, counting every possible downward transition among the levels.
questions.hint: Count all possible pairs of levels.
distractor_logic: only direct drops to each level

questions.question: The energy of the hydrogen electron in n = 2 is (E<sub>1</sub> = -2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> J):
questions.explanation: E<sub>n</sub> = -2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> / n<sup>2</sup> = -2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> / 4 = -0.545 × 10<sup>−18</sup> J.
questions.hint: Divide the ground state energy by n squared.
distractor_logic: sign flipped — bound states are negative

questions.question: The radius of Bohr's second orbit for hydrogen (a<sub>0</sub> = 52.9 pm) is:
questions.explanation: r<sub>n</sub> = n<sup>2</sup> a<sub>0</sub> = 4 × 52.9 = 211.6 pm.
questions.hint: Radius grows as n squared.

questions.question: Bohr's model could NOT explain:
options: The stability of the hydrogen atom
The spectrum of the helium atom
questions.explanation: Bohr works only for one-electron systems (H, He<sup>+</sup>, Li<sup>2+</sup>). It fails for multi-electron atoms like neutral He, and for the Zeeman and Stark effects.
questions.hint: Count the electrons in each option.

questions.question: Bohr's theory applies to He<sup>+</sup> and Li<sup>2+</sup> because they:
questions.explanation: He<sup>+</sup> and Li<sup>2+</sup> are hydrogen-like: one electron around the nucleus, so E_n = -2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> (Z<sup>2</sup>/n<sup>2</sup>) J applies.
questions.hint: What do they share with the hydrogen atom?

questions.question: The energy of the first orbit of He<sup>+</sup> is (Z = 2):
questions.explanation: E<sub>n</sub> = -2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> x Z<sup>2</sup>/n<sup>2</sup> = -2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> × 4 = -8.72 × 10<sup>−18</sup> J.
questions.hint: Energy scales with Z squared.

questions.question: The radius of the first orbit of He<sup>+</sup> is:
questions.explanation: r<sub>n</sub> = 52.9 n<sup>2</sup>/Z pm = 52.9/2 = 26.45 pm — higher nuclear charge pulls the electron closer.
questions.hint: Radius shrinks with increasing Z.

questions.question: The de Broglie wavelength of a 0.1 kg ball moving at 10 m/s is about:
questions.explanation: λ = h/mv = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup>/(0.1 × 10) = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup> m — absurdly small, which is why big objects show no wave behaviour.
questions.hint: mv = 1 kg m/s here, so λ = h numerically.

questions.question: Wave properties of ordinary objects (a cricket ball, a car) cannot be detected because:
options: Their large mass makes the wavelength immeasurably short
questions.explanation: λ = h/mv: large m gives wavelengths ~10<sup>−34</sup> m, far smaller than anything measurable. Electrons, with tiny mass, show detectable wavelengths.
questions.hint: Look at where mass sits in the de Broglie equation.

questions.question: An electron moving at 2.05 × 10<sup>7</sup> m/s has a de Broglie wavelength of about:
questions.explanation: λ = h/mv = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup>/(9.1 × 10<sup>−31</sup> × 2.05 × 10<sup>7</sup>) = 3.55 × 10<sup>−11</sup> m.
questions.hint: Divide h by (mass x velocity).

questions.question: The total number of orbitals associated with n = 3 is:
questions.explanation: Orbitals = n<sup>2</sup> = 9: one 3s + three 3p + five 3d.
questions.hint: Add 1 + 3 + 5, or square n.

questions.question: For n = 3, the possible values of l are:
questions.explanation: l runs from 0 to n-1, so for n = 3: l = 0 (3s), 1 (3p), 2 (3d).
questions.hint: l never reaches n.

questions.question: For l = 2, the possible values of m<sub>l</sub> are:
questions.explanation: m<sub>l</sub> = -l ... 0 ... +l, giving 2l+1 = 5 values — the five d orbitals.
questions.hint: There are 2l + 1 of them, symmetric about zero.

questions.question: The orbital with n = 4 and l = 0 is designated:
questions.explanation: l = 0 is always s; with n = 4 it is the 4s orbital. (l = 1: p, l = 2: d, l = 3: f.)
questions.hint: l = 0 has a one-letter name.

questions.question: Which of the following orbitals CANNOT exist?
questions.explanation: 1p needs l = 1 with n = 1 (impossible, l max = n-1 = 0); 3f needs l = 3 with n = 3 (impossible, l max = 2). The other pairs are all valid.
questions.hint: Check l ≤ n - 1 for each.

questions.question: The maximum number of electrons in a shell with principal quantum number n is:
questions.explanation: Each of the n<sup>2</sup> orbitals holds 2 electrons (Pauli), so the shell holds 2n<sup>2</sup> — e.g. 32 electrons for n = 4.
questions.hint: Orbitals in the shell times two.

questions.question: The number of radial nodes in a 3p orbital is:
questions.explanation: Radial nodes = n - l - 1 = 3 - 1 - 1 = 1. (Angular nodes = l = 1; total nodes = n - 1 = 2.)
questions.hint: Use n - l - 1.

questions.question: The number of angular nodes in any d orbital is:
questions.explanation: Angular nodes = l. For d orbitals l = 2, so two nodal planes pass through the nucleus (e.g. the two planes in dxy).
questions.hint: Angular nodes equal l.
distractor_logic: that's the number of d orbitals

questions.question: The 4s orbital is filled before 3d because:
questions.explanation: (n+l): 4s = 4+0 = 4; 3d = 3+2 = 5. Lower (n+l) means lower energy, so 4s fills first — K's valence electron sits in 4s, not 3d.
questions.hint: Apply the (n + l) rule.

questions.question: Immediately after 3p is filled, the next electron enters:
questions.explanation: Order: ...3p, 4s, 3d, 4p... 4s (n+l = 4) comes before 3d (n+l = 5). 3f doesn't exist at all.
questions.hint: The (n + l) rule decides.

questions.question: The observed valence configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is:
questions.explanation: An electron shifts from 4s to 3d to give the extra-stable half-filled 3d<sup>5</sup> — so Cr is [Ar]3d<sup>5</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>, not 3d<sup>4</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>.
questions.hint: Half-filled subshells have extra stability.

questions.question: Copper (Z = 29) adopts 3d<sup>10</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup> instead of 3d<sup>9</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> because:
options: Fully filled d subshells have extra stability
questions.explanation: Completely filled (d<sup>10</sup>) and half-filled (d<sup>5</sup>) subshells gain stability from symmetrical distribution and maximum exchange energy.
questions.hint: Same reason as chromium's exception.

questions.question: The number of unpaired electrons in phosphorus (Z = 15) is:
questions.explanation: P: [Ne]3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>3</sup>. By Hund's rule the three 3p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins — 3 unpaired.
questions.hint: Apply Hund's rule to 3p<sup>3</sup>.

questions.question: Hund's rule states that pairing of electrons in orbitals of the same subshell does not begin until:
options: Each orbital of the subshell is singly occupied
questions.explanation: Electrons first spread out one per degenerate orbital with parallel spins; pairing starts only after each orbital has one electron (4th electron in p, 6th in d).
questions.hint: Spread out first, pair later.

questions.question: The wavelength of light emitted when the hydrogen electron falls from n = 4 to n = 2 is about:
questions.explanation: ΔE = 2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> (1/4 - 1/16) = 4.09 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J; λ = hc/E = 1.986 × 10<sup>−25</sup>/4.09 × 10<sup>−19</sup> = 4.86 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m = 486 nm (Balmer, blue-green).
questions.hint: Compute ΔE first, then λ = hc/ΔE.

questions.question: The frequency of the photon emitted in the n = 5 to n = 2 transition of hydrogen is about:
questions.explanation: ΔE = 2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> (1/4 - 1/25) = 4.58 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J; ν = E/h = 6.91 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz (λ = 434 nm, visible Balmer line).
questions.hint: ν = ΔE / h.
distractor_logic: the energy value's digits reused as frequency

questions.question: The wavenumber of the LONGEST wavelength transition in the Balmer series is:
questions.explanation: Longest wavelength = smallest energy jump = n = 3 to 2: 109677(1/4 - 1/9) = 109677 × 5/36 = 15,233 cm<sup>−1</sup> (656 nm, the red H-α line).
questions.hint: The smallest jump into n = 2 gives the longest wavelength.

questions.question: The energy needed to ionise a hydrogen atom whose electron occupies n = 5, compared to ionisation from n = 1, is:
questions.explanation: Ionisation energy from level n is 2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup>/n<sup>2</sup>. From n = 5 it is 1/25 of the ground-state value (8.72 × 10<sup>−20</sup> J vs 2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> J).
questions.hint: Binding energy falls off as 1/n<sup>2</sup>.

questions.question: Which transition in the HYDROGEN spectrum has the same wavelength as the n = 4 to n = 2 Balmer transition of He<sup>+</sup>?
questions.explanation: For He<sup>+</sup>: wavenumber proportional to Z<sup>2</sup>(1/4 - 1/16) = 4 × 3/16 = 3/4. For H (Z = 1): need 1/n<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> - 1/n<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> = 3/4, which is 1/1 - 1/4 — the n = 2 to 1 transition.
questions.hint: Set Z<sup>2</sup> (1/n<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> - 1/n<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>) equal for both species.

questions.question: The energy required for He<sup>+</sup>(g) → He<sup>2+</sup>(g) + e<sup>−</sup> is (IE of H = 2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> J/atom):
questions.explanation: Ionising hydrogen-like He<sup>+</sup> from its ground state costs Z<sup>2</sup> times hydrogen's IE = 4 × 2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> = 8.72 × 10<sup>−18</sup> J.
questions.hint: One-electron ion: scale by Z squared.

questions.question: The number of photons of wavelength 4000 pm needed to provide 1 J of energy is about:
questions.explanation: E per photon = hc/λ = 1.986 × 10<sup>−25</sup>/4 × 10<sup>−9</sup> = 4.97 × 10<sup>−17</sup> J; N = 1/4.97 × 10<sup>−17</sup> = 2.01 × 10<sup>16</sup> photons.
questions.hint: Find one photon's energy, then divide 1 J by it.

questions.question: A 100 W bulb emits monochromatic light of wavelength 400 nm. The number of photons emitted per second is about:
questions.explanation: E per photon = hc/λ = 4.97 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J; photons/s = 100 J s<sup>−1</sup> / 4.97 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J = 2.012 × 10<sup>20</sup>.
questions.hint: Watts are joules per second — divide by one photon's energy.

questions.question: Radiation of 300 nm on sodium ejects electrons with kinetic energy 1.68 × 10<sup>5</sup> J/mol. The minimum energy needed to remove a mole of electrons from sodium is about:
questions.explanation: Energy of a mole of 300 nm photons = 3.99 × 10<sup>5</sup> J. Minimum (work function) = photon energy - KE = 3.99 - 1.68 = 2.31 × 10<sup>5</sup> J/mol.
questions.hint: Work function = photon energy minus kinetic energy.
distractor_logic: total photon energy, not the minimum

questions.question: Continuing the previous data (minimum energy 2.31 × 10<sup>5</sup> J/mol), the maximum wavelength that can still eject a photoelectron from sodium is about:
questions.explanation: Per electron: 2.31 × 10<sup>5</sup>/6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> = 3.84 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J; λ_max = hc/E = 1.986 × 10<sup>−25</sup>/3.84 × 10<sup>−19</sup> = 5.17 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m = 517 nm (green).
questions.hint: Threshold wavelength corresponds to exactly the work function.

questions.question: A metal has threshold frequency 7.0 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz. When radiation of 1.0 × 10<sup>15</sup> Hz hits it, the kinetic energy of an emitted electron is:
questions.explanation: KE = h(ν - &ν;<sub>0</sub>) = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup> x (10.0 - 7.0) x 10<sup>14</sup> = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup> × 3.0 × 10<sup>14</sup> = 1.988 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J.
questions.hint: Multiply h by the frequency EXCESS over threshold.

questions.question: An electron (m = 9.1 × 10<sup>−31</sup> kg) has kinetic energy 3.0 × 10<sup>−25</sup> J. Its de Broglie wavelength is about:
questions.explanation: v = √(2KE/m) = √(2 × 3.0 × 10<sup>−25</sup>/9.1 × 10<sup>−31</sup>) = 812 m/s; λ = h/mv = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup>/(9.1 × 10<sup>−31</sup> × 812) = 8.967 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m = 897 nm.
questions.hint: First get v from KE = (1/2)mv<sup>2</sup>, then λ = h/mv.

questions.question: A golf ball (40 g) moves at 45 m/s, speed known to 2%. The minimum uncertainty in its position is about:
questions.explanation: Δv = 0.9 m/s; Δx = h/(4 π m Δv) = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup>/(4 × 3.14 × 0.040 × 0.9) = 1.46 × 10<sup>−33</sup> m — ~10<sup>18</sup> times smaller than a nucleus, so meaningless for macroscopic objects.
questions.hint: Use Δx = h/(4 π m Δv) with mass in kg.

questions.question: If an electron's position is known within 0.1 Å, the minimum uncertainty in its velocity is about:
questions.explanation: Δv = h/(4 π m Δx) = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup>/(4 × 3.14 × 9.11 × 10<sup>−31</sup> × 10<sup>−11</sup>) = 5.79 × 10<sup>6</sup> m/s — enormous, so electron trajectories are meaningless.
questions.hint: Same relation, solved for Δv.

questions.question: The Bohr model contradicts the Heisenberg uncertainty principle because it:
options: Specifies an exact, fixed path (orbit) requiring exact position AND momentum simultaneously
questions.explanation: A defined circular orbit means position and velocity are both known exactly at every instant — precisely what the uncertainty principle forbids for an electron. Bohr also ignores the electron's wave character.
questions.hint: What information does a fixed circular path assume you have?

questions.question: The circumference of the nth Bohr orbit equals:
options: The de Broglie wavelength divided by n
n times the de Broglie wavelength of the electron
questions.explanation: From mvr = nh/2π: 2 π r = n(h/mv) = n λ. The orbit fits a whole number of electron wavelengths — a standing wave picture of quantisation.
questions.hint: Rearrange Bohr's angular momentum condition using λ = h/mv.
distractor_logic: confused with r proportional to n<sup>2</sup>

questions.question: The total number of nodes in a 4d orbital is:
questions.explanation: Total nodes = n - 1 = 3: angular nodes = l = 2, radial nodes = n - l - 1 = 1.
questions.hint: Total is n - 1; split it into angular (l) and radial (n - l - 1).

questions.question: How many electrons in an atom can have n = 4 and m<sub>s</sub> = -1/2?
questions.explanation: The n = 4 shell has n<sup>2</sup> = 16 orbitals holding 32 electrons; exactly half of them (one per orbital) have m<sub>s</sub> = -1/2, i.e. 16.
questions.hint: Half the shell's capacity.

questions.question: An atom contains 29 electrons and 35 neutrons. Its electronic configuration is:
questions.explanation: 29 electrons = copper. Cu takes the exceptional configuration [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup> for full-d stability. (Z = 29, A = 64.)
questions.hint: Identify the element first, then recall its exceptional configuration.

questions.question: The lowest value of n that allows g orbitals (l = 4) to exist is:
questions.explanation: l max = n - 1, so l = 4 first becomes possible at n = 5 (the 5g subshell).
questions.hint: l can go up to n - 1.

questions.question: An element with mass number 81 contains 31.7% more neutrons than protons. The element is:
questions.explanation: n = 1.317p and p + n = 81 gives 2.317p = 81, p = 35 (Br), n = 46. So the nuclide is <sup>81</sup>Br.
questions.hint: Set n = 1.317p and solve p + n = 81.

questions.question: An ion with mass number 37 has one unit of negative charge and 11.1% more neutrons than electrons. The ion is:
questions.explanation: Let electrons = e; neutrons = 1.111e; protons = e - 1. Then (e-1) + 1.111e = 37 gives e = 18, n = 20, p = 17 — chlorine, so <sup>37</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup>.
questions.hint: For a -1 ion, protons = electrons - 1.

questions.question: An ion with mass number 56 carries 3 units of positive charge and has 30.4% more neutrons than electrons. The ion is:
questions.explanation: Electrons = e; neutrons = 1.304e; protons = e + 3. (e+3) + 1.304e = 56 gives e = 23, n = 30, p = 26 — iron, so <sup>56</sup>Fe<sup>3+</sup>.
questions.hint: For a +3 ion, protons = electrons + 3.

questions.question: The diameter of a zinc atom is 2.6 Å. The number of zinc atoms arranged side by side lengthwise in 1.6 cm is about:
questions.explanation: N = length/diameter = 1.6 × 10<sup>−2</sup> m / 2.6 × 10<sup>−10</sup> m = 6.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> atoms. (Radius = 130 pm.)
questions.hint: Divide total length by one atom's DIAMETER.

questions.question: 2 × 10<sup>8</sup> carbon atoms arranged side by side span 2.4 cm. The radius of a carbon atom is:
questions.explanation: Diameter = 2.4 × 10<sup>−2</sup>/2 × 10<sup>8</sup> = 1.2 × 10<sup>−10</sup> m = 0.12 nm; radius = 0.06 nm (60 pm).
questions.hint: Length over count gives the diameter — halve it.

questions.question: A particle carries 2.5 × 10<sup>−16</sup> C of static charge. The number of electrons on it is about:
questions.explanation: N = q/e = 2.5 × 10<sup>−16</sup>/1.602 × 10<sup>−19</sup> = 1560 electrons — an integer multiple, as Millikan's q = ne demands.
questions.hint: Divide the total charge by the electron's charge.

questions.question: In Millikan's experiment an oil drop carries -1.282 × 10<sup>−18</sup> C. The number of electrons on the drop is:
questions.explanation: N = 1.282 × 10<sup>−18</sup>/1.602 × 10<sup>−19</sup> = 8.00 — exactly 8 electrons. A non-integer answer would signal an arithmetic error, since charge comes only in whole multiples of e.
questions.hint: The answer must be a whole number.

questions.question: Among 3p, 3d and 4s in a multi-electron atom, the orbital with the LOWEST energy is:
questions.explanation: (n+l): 3p = 4, 4s = 4, 3d = 5. Between 3p and 4s (tie), the lower n wins — 3p is lowest, then 4s, then 3d.
questions.hint: Compute (n + l) for each; break ties with n.

questions.question: A Paschen series transition (ending at n = 3) is observed at 1285 nm. It starts from n =
questions.explanation: ν = c/λ = 2.335 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz. Using ν = 3.29 × 10<sup>15</sup> (1/9 - 1/n<sup>2</sup>): 1/9 - 1/n<sup>2</sup> = 0.071, so 1/n<sup>2</sup> = 0.040, n<sup>2</sup> = 25, n = 5. Region: infrared.
questions.hint: Convert to frequency, then solve the Rydberg expression for n.

questions.question: An emission transition starts from an orbit of radius 1.3225 nm and ends at 211.6 pm. The transition and its series are:
questions.explanation: r = n<sup>2</sup> × 52.9 pm: 1322.5 pm gives n = 5; 211.6 pm gives n = 2. So 5 → 2 — a Balmer line (434 nm, visible).
questions.hint: Divide each radius by 52.9 pm and take the square root.

questions.question: Which species in which state has the SAME energy as a hydrogen atom in its ground state (n = 1)?
questions.explanation: E is proportional to Z<sup>2</sup>/n<sup>2</sup>. For H(n=1): 1/1 = 1. He<sup>+</sup>(n=2): 4/4 = 1 — equal. Li<sup>2+</sup>(n=2) gives 9/4, He<sup>+</sup>(n=4) gives 4/16.
questions.hint: Compare Z<sup>2</sup>/n<sup>2</sup> for each option.

questions.question: The ratio of the radius of the n = 2 orbit of H to that of the n = 2 orbit of He<sup>+</sup> is:
questions.explanation: r proportional to n<sup>2</sup>/Z. Same n, so ratio = Z(He<sup>+</sup>)/Z(H) = 2:1 — the He<sup>+</sup> orbit is half as large.
questions.hint: Radius shrinks with nuclear charge.

questions.question: The electron in Bohr's first orbit moves at 2.19 × 10<sup>6</sup> m/s. Its de Broglie wavelength is about:
questions.explanation: λ = h/mv = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup>/(9.1 × 10<sup>−31</sup> × 2.19 × 10<sup>6</sup>) = 3.32 × 10<sup>−10</sup> m = 332 pm — exactly the circumference of the first Bohr orbit (2 π x 52.9 pm), as the standing-wave condition requires.
questions.hint: It should equal 2 π times the Bohr radius.

questions.question: A 150 pm photon strikes an atom and an inner electron is ejected at 1.5 × 10<sup>7</sup> m/s. The energy binding the electron to the nucleus was about:
questions.explanation: Photon energy = hc/λ = 1.325 × 10<sup>−15</sup> J. KE = (1/2)(9.1 × 10<sup>−31</sup>)(1.5 × 10<sup>7</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = 1.02 × 10<sup>−16</sup> J. Binding energy = 1.325 × 10<sup>−15</sup> - 1.02 × 10<sup>−16</sup> = 1.22 × 10<sup>−15</sup> J.
questions.hint: Binding energy = photon energy minus kinetic energy.

questions.question: Neon sign light at 616 nm has frequency:
questions.explanation: ν = c/λ = 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup>/616 × 10<sup>−9</sup> = 4.87 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz.
questions.hint: c over λ in metres.

questions.question: If that same 616 nm neon emission delivers 2 J of energy, the number of quanta involved is about:
questions.explanation: E per quantum = hc/λ = 3.23 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J; N = 2/3.23 × 10<sup>−19</sup> = 6.2 × 10<sup>18</sup> quanta.
questions.hint: Total energy divided by the energy of one quantum.

questions.question: A photon detector receives 3.15 × 10<sup>−18</sup> J in total from 600 nm starlight. The number of photons received is:
questions.explanation: E per photon = hc/λ = 3.31 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J; N = 3.15 × 10<sup>−18</sup>/3.31 × 10<sup>−19</sup> = 9.5, i.e. about 10 photons — astronomy really does count single photons.
questions.hint: The answer is a surprisingly small whole number.

questions.question: A nitrogen laser at 337.1 nm emits 5.6 × 10<sup>24</sup> photons. The total energy is about:
questions.explanation: E per photon = hc/λ = 5.9 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J; total = 5.9 × 10<sup>−19</sup> × 5.6 × 10<sup>24</sup> = 3.3 × 10<sup>6</sup> J.
questions.hint: One photon's energy times the photon count.

questions.question: The sodium doublet lines lie at 589.0 and 589.6 nm. The energy DIFFERENCE between the two excited states is about:
options: Zero — they are the same state
questions.explanation: nu1 = 5.093 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz, nu2 = 5.088 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz; Δν = 5.2 × 10<sup>11</sup> Hz, so ΔE = h Δν = 3.45 × 10<sup>−22</sup> J — tiny, which is why the lines sit so close.
questions.hint: Work with the difference in frequencies, not either frequency alone.
distractor_logic: the doublet exists because they differ

questions.question: The work function of caesium is 1.9 eV. Its threshold wavelength is about (1 eV = 1.602 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J):
questions.explanation: W<sub>0</sub> = 3.04 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J; λ0 = hc/W<sub>0</sub> = 1.986 × 10<sup>−25</sup>/3.04 × 10<sup>−19</sup> = 6.53 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m = 653 nm — red light can just barely eject electrons from Cs.
questions.hint: λ0 = hc / work function (in joules).

questions.question: Given work functions Li 2.42, Na 2.3, K 2.25, Cu 4.8, Ag 4.3 eV — which metal needs light of the HIGHEST frequency to show the photoelectric effect?
questions.explanation: Threshold frequency &ν;<sub>0</sub> = W<sub>0</sub>/h, so the largest work function (Cu, 4.8 eV) demands the highest frequency; K (2.25 eV) is the easiest.
questions.hint: Bigger energy barrier means higher frequency needed.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT isoelectronic with argon (18 e)?
questions.explanation: K<sup>+</sup> (19-1), Ca<sup>2+</sup> (20-2) and S<sup>2−</sup> (16+2) all have 18 electrons. Na<sup>+</sup> has 10 — isoelectronic with neon instead.
questions.hint: Do the electron count for each ion.

questions.question: The electronic configuration of Fe<sup>3+</sup> (Fe: Z = 26) is:
questions.explanation: Fe = [Ar]3d<sup>6</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>. Cations lose the OUTERMOST (4s) electrons first, then one 3d: Fe<sup>3+</sup> = [Ar]3d<sup>5</sup> — extra stable because half-filled.
questions.hint: 4s electrons leave before 3d when forming cations.

questions.question: The number of unpaired electrons in iron (Z = 26, [Ar]3d<sup>6</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>) is:
questions.explanation: In 3d<sup>6</sup>, five electrons singly occupy the five d orbitals (Hund), and the sixth pairs up in one of them — leaving 4 unpaired.
questions.hint: Fill five d boxes by Hund's rule, then add the sixth electron.

questions.question: The number of unpaired electrons in chromium ([Ar]3d<sup>5</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>) is:
questions.explanation: All five 3d electrons are unpaired (half-filled) AND the lone 4s electron is unpaired: total 6 — the maximum for any element up to Z = 30.
questions.hint: Don't forget the 4s electron.

questions.question: Half-filled and fully filled subshells are extra stable because of symmetrical electron distribution and maximum:
questions.explanation: Electrons of the same spin in degenerate orbitals can exchange positions, releasing exchange energy — maximised when the subshell is exactly half or completely filled.
questions.hint: Same-spin electrons swapping positions releases this energy.

questions.question: The atomic number of the element whose outermost electrons are 3p<sup>5</sup> is:
questions.explanation: Count up to 3p<sup>5</sup>: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 17 — chlorine. (3s fills before 3p.)
questions.hint: Add all electrons through [Ne]3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>5</sup>.

questions.question: The atom with configuration [Ne] 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>3</sup> is:
questions.explanation: 10 (Ne core) + 2 + 3 = 15 electrons = phosphorus. Nitrogen is [He]2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>3</sup> — same group, one period up.
questions.hint: Count total electrons including the core.

questions.question: Which set of quantum numbers is NOT possible?
questions.explanation: For n = 1, l can only be 0; l = 1 requires n ≥ 2. All other sets satisfy l ≤ n-1 and |m<sub>l</sub>| ≤ l.
questions.hint: Check l against n - 1 in each set.

questions.question: Which set of quantum numbers is NOT possible?
questions.explanation: l runs only up to n - 1 = 2 for n = 3, so l = 3 (an 'f' subshell in the third shell) cannot exist.
questions.hint: l must stay below n.

questions.question: An electron is in a 3d orbital. Its n and l values are:
questions.explanation: The digit is n = 3; the letter d means l = 2 (m<sub>l</sub> can be -2 to +2).
questions.hint: s, p, d, f correspond to l = 0, 1, 2, 3.

questions.question: The maximum number of electrons in the 3s subshell is ______ and in the 3d subshell is ______.
questions.explanation: s has 1 orbital (2 electrons); d has 5 orbitals (10 electrons). Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons with opposite spins (Pauli).
questions.hint: Orbitals in the subshell times two.

questions.question: 2p and 3s have (n+l) = 3 and 3, yet 2p fills first because:
options: It is closer to the nucleus in every atom
p orbitals are always lower than s
When (n+l) is equal, the orbital with lower n has lower energy
questions.explanation: The tie-break of the (n+l) rule: equal (n+l) means the smaller n wins — 2p (n = 2) is lower in energy than 3s (n = 3).
questions.hint: The rule has a second clause for ties.

questions.question: Between 3p and 3d electrons in the same atom, the 3p electron experiences a LARGER effective nuclear charge because it:
options: Penetrates closer to the nucleus and is less shielded
questions.explanation: Within a shell, penetration decreases s > p > d > f; the 3p electron spends more time near the nucleus, feels a higher Zeff, and is more tightly bound than 3d.
questions.hint: Think about which orbital spends more time near the nucleus.

questions.question: Among 4d and 4f in the same atom, the larger effective nuclear charge is experienced by the electron in:
questions.explanation: Penetration order s > p > d > f: 4d penetrates more than 4f, is less shielded, and feels the larger Zeff.
questions.hint: The earlier letter in s, p, d, f penetrates more.

questions.question: The unpaired 3p electrons of Al (Z = 13) and Si (Z = 14) — which feel more effective nuclear charge?
questions.explanation: Same subshell, but Si has one more proton; nuclear charge rises faster than the extra shielding from one more 3p electron, so Si's 3p electrons feel the higher Zeff.
questions.hint: Compare the nuclear charges.
distractor_logic: shielding doesn't fully cancel the extra proton

questions.question: In bromine (Z = 35), which electrons experience the LOWEST effective nuclear charge: those in 2p, 3p or 4p?
questions.explanation: The 4p electrons are the outermost — screened by all the inner shells — so they feel the smallest net pull. Zeff decreases outward: 2p > 3p > 4p.
questions.hint: The most-shielded, outermost electrons feel the least.

questions.question: The number of spectral lines produced when a hydrogen electron drops from n = 4 to the ground state is:
questions.hint: Count every possible downward hop, not just direct ones.

questions.question: The series limit (shortest wavelength) of the Lyman series has wavenumber:
questions.explanation: Series limit: n<sub>2</sub> = ∞, so wavenumber = 109677(1/1 - 0) = 109677 cm<sup>−1</sup> (about 91.2 nm) — the full Rydberg constant.
questions.hint: Set n<sub>2</sub> to ∞ with n<sub>1</sub> = 1.

questions.question: An absorption spectrum is described as the ______ of the emission spectrum.
questions.explanation: The wavelengths absorbed (dark lines on a bright continuum) are exactly those emitted (bright lines on dark) — NCERT calls it the photographic negative.
questions.hint: Dark lines where the other has bright ones.

questions.question: The energy required to shift the hydrogen electron from n = 1 to n = 5 is about:
questions.explanation: ΔE = 2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> (1/1 - 1/25) = 2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> × 0.96 = 2.09 × 10<sup>−18</sup> J — nearly the full ionisation energy.
questions.hint: It's slightly LESS than the ionisation energy.

questions.question: When that electron (n = 5) returns to the ground state, the emitted light has wavelength about:
questions.explanation: λ = hc/ΔE = 1.986 × 10<sup>−25</sup>/2.09 × 10<sup>−18</sup> = 9.5 × 10<sup>−8</sup> m = 95 nm — ultraviolet, a Lyman series line.
questions.hint: Any drop to n = 1 lands in the ultraviolet.

questions.question: The longest wavelength of light that can just remove the electron from the n = 2 level of hydrogen is about:
questions.explanation: E needed = 2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup>/4 = 5.45 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J; λ = hc/E = 1.986 × 10<sup>−25</sup>/5.45 × 10<sup>−19</sup> = 3.65 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m = 365 nm.
questions.hint: Ionisation from n = 2 costs a quarter of the ground-state IE.

questions.question: In a neutron diffraction microscope the wavelength used is 800 pm. The neutron's velocity (m = 1.675 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg) is about:
questions.explanation: v = h/(m λ) = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup>/(1.675 × 10<sup>−27</sup> × 8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>) = 494 m/s.
questions.hint: Rearrange de Broglie for v.

questions.question: An electron and a proton have the SAME de Broglie wavelength. Which is moving faster?
questions.explanation: λ = h/mv: equal λ means equal momentum mv. The electron, being ~1836 times lighter, must move ~1836 times faster.
questions.hint: Equal wavelength means equal momentum.

questions.question: In an electron microscope the electrons move at 1.6 × 10<sup>6</sup> m/s. Their de Broglie wavelength is about:
questions.explanation: λ = h/mv = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup>/(9.1 × 10<sup>−31</sup> × 1.6 × 10<sup>6</sup>) = 4.55 × 10<sup>−10</sup> m = 455 pm — short enough to resolve molecules, the basis of electron microscopy.
questions.hint: Same calculation as any de Broglie problem.

questions.question: The total number of electrons present in one mole of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) is:
questions.explanation: CH<sub>4</sub> has 6 + 4 = 10 electrons per molecule; per mole: 10 × 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> = 6.022 × 10<sup>24</sup>.
questions.hint: Electrons per molecule times Avogadro's number.

questions.question: The number of electrons that together weigh one gram is about:
questions.explanation: N = 10<sup>−3</sup> kg / 9.109 × 10<sup>−31</sup> kg = 1.098 × 10<sup>27</sup> electrons — far more than a mole, because electrons are so light.
questions.hint: Divide 1 g (in kg) by one electron's mass.

questions.question: Arrange in INCREASING order of frequency: FM radio, microwave (oven), amber traffic light, X-rays.
questions.explanation: Radio (~10<sup>8</sup> Hz) < microwave (~10<sup>10</sup>) < visible amber (~10<sup>14</sup>) < X-rays (~10<sup>18</sup>). Cosmic rays would sit even higher.
questions.hint: Longer wavelength means lower frequency.

questions.question: For a milligram-scale object, Δv x Δx is about 10<sup>−28</sup> m<sup>2</sup>/s, but for an electron it is about 10<sup>−4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>/s. The correct conclusion is:
options: Uncertainty is negligible for macroscopic objects but decisive for electrons
The principle fails for small masses
questions.explanation: The h/(4 π m) product is inversely proportional to mass: insignificant for milligram objects, enormous for electrons — which is exactly why electron trajectories (Bohr orbits) are replaced by probability statements in the quantum mechanical model.
questions.hint: Compare the two magnitudes against real measurement scales.

topics.name: Subatomic Particles
topics.summary: Atoms are built from three particles. Electrons (found via cathode rays; charge −1.602 × 10−19 C by Millikan's oil drop, mass 9.109 × 10−31 kg) are negative and very light. Protons (the H+ ion, from canal rays) are positive with mass ≈ 1 u. Neutrons (Chadwick, 1932 — α-particles on beryllium) are neutral, slightly heavier than protons. Thomson measured e/m of the electron with crossed electric and magnetic fields; combining it with Millikan's e gave the electron's mass.
topics.worked_example: A drop carries −1.282 × 10<sup>−18</sup> C. Electrons on it = 1.282 × 10<sup>−18</sup> / 1.602 × 10<sup>−19</sup> = 8 — always a whole number.
common_mistakes: Mixing up which scientist did which experiment (Thomson: e/m, Millikan: e, Chadwick: neutron)
Confusing the electron's mass and charge values
Forgetting charge comes only in whole multiples of e

topics.name: Atomic Models
topics.summary: Thomson (1898): a uniform positive sphere with electrons embedded — the plum-pudding model; mass spread evenly. Rutherford (1909) shot α-particles at thin gold foil: most passed straight through, a few deflected, ~1 in 20,000 bounced back. Conclusion: nearly all mass and all positive charge sit in a tiny nucleus (~10−15 m) inside a mostly empty atom (~10−10 m), with electrons orbiting like planets. Fatal flaw: an orbiting (accelerating) charge should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus in ~10−8 s — Rutherford's model cannot explain atomic stability.
topics.worked_example: If the nucleus were a cricket ball, the atom would be about 5 km wide — that's how empty the atom is.
common_mistakes: Saying Rutherford's model explains stability (it's exactly what it fails at)
Thinking many α-particles bounced back — it was extremely rare
Confusing which model assumes uniformly spread mass (Thomson)

topics.name: Atomic Number & Mass Number
topics.summary: Atomic number Z = protons in the nucleus = electrons in a neutral atom; it defines the element. Mass number A = protons + neutrons (together: nucleons). Notation: AZX. For ions, count carefully: an anion has MORE electrons than protons; a cation has fewer. Neutrons = A − Z always, ion or not.
topics.worked_example: Species with 18 e, 16 p, 16 n: Z = 16 → sulphur; 2 extra electrons → S<sup>2−</sup>; A = 32.
common_mistakes: Using electron count to identify the element of an ion (protons decide the element)
Forgetting anion = extra electrons, cation = missing electrons
Swapping A and Z in the symbol

topics.name: Isotopes & Isobars
topics.summary: Isotopes: same Z, different A — same element with different neutron counts (protium 1H, deuterium 2D, tritium 3T; or 12C, 13C, 14C). All isotopes of an element show the SAME chemical behaviour because chemistry is controlled by electrons, whose number is fixed by protons. Isobars: same A, different Z — different elements, e.g. 14C and 14N.
topics.worked_example: Tritium = 1 proton + 2 neutrons, so A = 3. Deuterium has 1 neutron, protium none.
common_mistakes: Swapping the definitions of isotopes and isobars
Expecting isotopes to differ chemically (they don't — neutrons barely affect chemistry)

topics.name: Electromagnetic Radiation
topics.summary: Light is oscillating electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel; no medium needed. In vacuum ALL EM waves travel at c = 3.0 × 108 m/s. A wave is described by frequency ν (waves per second, in Hz), wavelength λ, and wavenumber (wavelengths per unit length, = 1/λ, usually cm−1). The spectrum runs radio → microwave → IR → visible (400–750 nm) → UV → X-rays → γ-rays, in increasing frequency.
common_mistakes: Not converting nm/Å/pm to metres before using c = νλ
Inverting the relation (dividing when you should multiply)
Ordering the spectrum by wavelength when asked for frequency

topics.name: Planck's Quantum Theory
topics.summary: Hot-body radiation couldn't be explained by wave theory. Planck (1900): energy is emitted or absorbed only in discrete packets — quanta — with E = hν, h = 6.626 × 10−34 J s. Energy is like a staircase, not a ramp: only 0, hν, 2hν... are allowed. For light the quantum is the photon. Total energy of N photons = Nhν; a mole of photons carries NAhν.
topics.worked_example: Photons/second from a 100 W, 400 nm bulb: E<sub>photon</sub> = hc/λ = 4.97 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J; N = 100 / 4.97 × 10<sup>−19</sup> = 2.01 × 10<sup>20</sup> per second.
common_mistakes: Forgetting Avogadro's number when moving between one photon and a mole
Using λ where ν belongs (E = hν, not hλ)
Power-of-ten slips with nm → m conversion

topics.name: Photoelectric Effect
topics.summary: Light of high enough frequency ejects electrons from a metal instantly. Three facts wave theory can't explain: (1) no time lag; (2) below a threshold frequency ν0 nothing is ejected however bright the light; (3) kinetic energy of ejected electrons grows with FREQUENCY, while their NUMBER grows with intensity. Einstein (1905): one photon gives all its energy hν to one electron; hν0 (the work function W0) pays the escape cost and the rest becomes kinetic energy.
topics.worked_example: ν<sub>0</sub> = 7.0 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz, light of 1.0 × 10<sup>15</sup> Hz: KE = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup> × 3.0 × 10<sup>14</sup> = 1.99 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J.
common_mistakes: Using the full ν instead of (ν − ν<sub>0</sub>) for KE
Thinking brighter light raises each electron's KE (it only raises the count)
Believing intense below-threshold light eventually works (it never does)

topics.name: Atomic Spectra
topics.summary: White light gives a continuous spectrum; excited gas atoms emit only specific wavelengths — a line (emission) spectrum, unique to each element like a fingerprint. An absorption spectrum is its photographic negative: dark lines on a continuum at the same wavelengths. Hydrogen's lines form series: Lyman (to n=1, UV), Balmer (to n=2, visible), Paschen/Brackett/Pfund (to n=3,4,5, IR), all fitting Rydberg's formula. Dropping from level n gives n(n−1)/2 possible lines.
topics.worked_example: Longest Balmer wavelength = smallest jump (3→2): 109677 × (1/4 − 1/9) = 15,233 cm<sup>−1</sup> — the red H-α line at 656 nm.
common_mistakes: Longest wavelength means SMALLEST energy jump, not largest
Assigning series to wrong regions (only Balmer is visible)
Counting only direct drops instead of all n(n−1)/2 transitions

topics.name: Bohr Model
topics.summary: Bohr (1913) for hydrogen: electrons move only in fixed orbits where angular momentum mevr = nh/2π. Each orbit has fixed energy En = −2.18 × 10−18/n2 J and radius rn = 52.9 n2 pm. Energy is negative because the bound electron is lower than a free one (E = 0 at n = ∞). Jumps between orbits absorb/emit photons: ΔE = hν. Works for any ONE-electron species (He+, Li2+) with E ∝ Z2/n2, r ∝ n2/Z. Fails for multi-electron atoms, Zeeman/Stark effects — and contradicts wave nature and uncertainty.
common_mistakes: Forgetting Z<sup>2</sup> for He<sup>+</sup>/Li<sup>2+</sup> (or using Z instead of Z<sup>2</sup>)
Dropping the negative sign's meaning — more negative = more stable
Confusing r ∝ n<sup>2</sup> with r ∝ n

topics.name: Dual Nature & de Broglie
topics.summary: Light behaves as wave (interference, diffraction) AND particle (photoelectric effect). de Broglie (1924): matter does too — every moving particle has wavelength λ = h/mv. For everyday objects the mass is so large that λ (~10−34 m) is undetectable; for electrons it's comparable to atomic sizes, which is why electron beams diffract and electron microscopes work. In Bohr's orbits, 2πr = nλ — a whole number of electron waves fits each allowed orbit.
common_mistakes: Equal λ means equal MOMENTUM, so the lighter particle moves faster
Forgetting to get v from KE first when only energy is given
Power-of-ten slips with the tiny masses

topics.name: Heisenberg Uncertainty
topics.summary: Heisenberg (1927): position and momentum (or velocity) of a particle cannot both be known exactly at the same time: Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π. The h/4πm factor makes this meaningless for milligram-and-heavier objects but decisive for electrons — pin an electron's position to 0.1 Å and its velocity is uncertain by ~5.8 × 106 m/s. Consequence: electrons have no definite paths, so Bohr's fixed orbits are impossible; the quantum model replaces trajectories with probabilities.
topics.worked_example: Golf ball, 40 g, Δv = 0.9 m/s: Δx = h/(4π × 0.040 × 0.9) = 1.46 × 10<sup>−33</sup> m — ~10<sup>18</sup> times smaller than a nucleus, hence irrelevant.
common_mistakes: Forgetting mass sits in the denominator (small mass = big uncertainty)
Leaving mass in grams instead of kg
Treating the principle as a measurement flaw rather than a fundamental limit

topics.name: Quantum Numbers
topics.summary: Each orbital is labelled by three quantum numbers: n (1, 2, 3... — shell, size, mostly energy), l (0 to n−1 — subshell and shape: s, p, d, f for l = 0, 1, 2, 3), and ml (−l to +l — orientation; 2l+1 orbitals per subshell). A fourth, spin ms = +½ or −½, belongs to the electron. Validity checks: l < n always; |ml| ≤ l. Shell capacities: n2 orbitals, 2n2 electrons.
topics.worked_example: Is n = 3, l = 3 allowed? No — l max = n − 1 = 2, so 3f doesn't exist; 3s, 3p, 3d do.
common_mistakes: Allowing l = n (1p, 3f are impossible)
Listing m<sub>l</sub> as only positive values
Confusing n<sup>2</sup> (orbitals) with 2n<sup>2</sup> (electrons)

topics.name: Orbitals & Shapes
topics.summary: An orbital is the wave function ψ of an electron; |ψ|2 is the probability density of finding it. s orbitals are spherical; p orbitals are dumbbells along x, y, z; d orbitals (five) are mostly double dumbbells. Nodes are zero-probability regions: radial nodes = n − l − 1, angular nodes (planes) = l, total = n − 1. Within a shell, penetration s > p > d > f: more-penetrating electrons feel a larger effective nuclear charge Zeff and sit lower in energy; outer electrons are shielded by inner shells.
common_mistakes: Mixing radial and angular node formulas
Thinking orbit and orbital are the same thing (they are not)
Reversing the penetration order s > p > d > f

topics.name: Electronic Configuration
topics.summary: Electrons fill orbitals by three rules. Aufbau: lowest energy first, ordered by the (n+l) rule — lower (n+l) fills first; on a tie, lower n wins (so 4s before 3d, 2p before 3s... order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s...). Pauli: no two electrons share all four quantum numbers — max 2 per orbital, opposite spins. Hund: within a subshell, one electron per orbital (parallel spins) before any pairing. Exceptions: Cr = [Ar]3d54s1, Cu = [Ar]3d104s1 — half-filled and fully filled subshells gain extra stability from symmetry and exchange energy. Cations lose 4s electrons before 3d.
key_formulas: max electrons: s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14
topics.worked_example: Fe = [Ar]3d<sup>6</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> → Fe<sup>3+</sup> = [Ar]3d<sup>5</sup> (4s pair leaves first, then one 3d) — half-filled, extra stable, 5 unpaired electrons.
common_mistakes: Writing Cr/Cu by naive aufbau (3d<sup>4</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>, 3d<sup>9</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> are wrong)
Removing 3d electrons before 4s when forming cations
Pairing electrons before every orbital of the subshell is singly filled
